source.title: Note on Selection Bias in Observational Estimates of Algorithmic Progress

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper derives and simulates how selection between dataset size and latent algorithmic quality can bias fitted estimates of algorithmic progress, refining the scope of observational estimates.
record.gate_note: The paper takes a scaling-law equation as its starting point but does not test whether language-model loss follows power laws, whether small runs extrapolate to larger runs, or how compute-optimal allocations scale. Its own theorem and Monte Carlo results concern bias in an observational estimate of algorithmic progress. Comparisons of beta estimates attributed to Ho et al., Hoffmann et al. and Besiroglu et al. are cited results, not findings newly produced by this paper.
record.test_reason: This is a theoretical and Monte Carlo econometrics note on Ho et al. (2024). It assumes a Chinchilla-style power law as the data-generating process and shows that selection between latent algorithmic quality and dataset size biases OLS estimates of beta and of the algorithmic-progress rate. It trains no models and fits no new language-model loss data. Its only real-data comparison (beta about 0.37 experimental vs 0.04 observational) is cited from other papers. The argument fits V7's theme that fitting choices change exponents, but its own results are derived from an assumed process, so they cannot show whether any version holds for real language models. I record it as discussion, not a test.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The author argues that compute choices made endogenously to latent algorithmic quality bias observational estimates of algorithmic progress, in Ho et al. and in general. A first-pass comparison suggests progress may be overstated about ninefold, though the author flags this as very rough. The author proposes experimental assignment or an instrument as remedies.
record.recipe_differences: Uses an omitted-variable-bias analysis and Monte Carlo simulations of an observational estimator, rather than training language models across parameter, data or compute scales and measuring held-out loss.
record.method_sensitivity: The simulated estimate changes with the correlation between latent productivity and log dataset size. The authors also caution that exact magnitudes are sensitive to the chosen distribution, especially its variance.

fits_no_version.finding: Under an assumed power-law process, latent lab-level algorithmic quality correlated with dataset size biases observational OLS estimates. Theorem 1: the progress-rate bias has the opposite sign to Cov(ln D, eps_D). Monte Carlo with true 45% annual progress gives estimates of 16.5% at correlation 0.5 and 93% at -0.5.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Observational, cross-lab fits of scaling-law parameters (data exponent, algorithmic-progress rate) are biased by endogenous compute choices, unlike experimental fits with algorithms held fixed.

record.problems: The Monte Carlo magnitudes depend on the chosen error distribution and variance, and the paper says not to take the exact magnitudes too seriously. The paper does not empirically establish the size or sign of selection bias in real language-model data.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. The cited estimates β around 0.37 and β around 0.04 are attributed to other studies and were not newly produced here.

untested.parts: All; the power law is assumed as the data-generating process.
No empirical test of how exponents depend on setup or fitting choices. The 0.37 vs 0.04 beta gap is cited from Hoffmann, Besiroglu and Ho et al., not produced here.

missing.what: Appendix derivation: the fitted beta itself is biased by a term proportional to Cov(ln D, eps_D). This is a theoretical result on the exponent estimate, relevant context for V7.

record.verdict_notes: Reader's 'tests/T5' with a V7 'supports' label is overturned. The study's own results are simulated or theoretical under an assumed power law, and the only empirical exponent comparison is cited, so no verdict is given. Its theme is consistent with V7, but this is not independent evidence for it.

versions.untested_parts: Whether held-out loss follows power laws in parameters, tokens or compute.
Whether fits from small runs predict much larger runs.
Whether compute-optimal parameter and token counts grow as stable powers of compute.
Whether architecture details have little effect at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability of downstream-task performance from scale or pretraining loss.

Tests sensitivity of an estimated algorithmic-progress rate to selection in a specified observational regression. Does not test fitted loss-scaling exponents, compute-optimal allocations, curve bending, or empirical disagreement between power-law fits.
